candidates.why: Well-controlled 6-model/30-round study with an item-level decomposition, but the area's cap is taken by the far larger 1,030-run reproducibility audit; SkillDiff's gain is reported as bare point deltas.
candidates.caveat: SkillDiff's evaluation is point deltas only — no confidence intervals, no repeated runs, no per-task breakdown.

candidates.why: 1,030 evolution runs and 2.1M trajectories show headline agent-evolution gains largely vanish once the grader is repaired, with power analysis on how many runs a real 3.4-pp effect needs.
candidates.caveat: The 'selection ≈ chance' conclusion is barely identified — false-acceptance intervals are enormous (62.1% ± 42.9).

candidates.why: Huge factorial (1.87M executions) and the format-rescoring insight is valuable, but H2 bundles feedback with retries and the rescue regime is a single model.
candidates.caveat: H2 is a bundle — error feedback plus up to three bounded retries are never separated.

candidates.why: Regime-change observation is interesting but rests on one 76.8M trajectory with correlated checkpoints, and learning rate alone already correlates r=0.984 with the score.
candidates.caveat: The main evidence is one 76.8M trajectory with ten nearby checkpoints that share history.

candidates.why: Honest negative result on router collapse, but a single 4-class IEMOCAP setup with a confounded intervention and no accuracy or stability gain.
candidates.caveat: The intervention is confounded — the fused representation feeds both the router and the experts.

candidates.why: Zero-parameter fix is cheap, but the deltas are ~0.004 nats and the guarantees hold only in a narrow contraction regime.
candidates.caveat: Theorem 2.2 promises strictly positive mixing, but at the recommended λ=0.97 with small K that guarantee is thin.

candidates.why: A pre-training audit (verifier false-positive rate × starting-policy exposure) predicts which loophole RL exploits first at AUROC 0.974, ranks the winner first in 12/12 runs, and transfers to held-out judges.
candidates.caveat: The causal claim rests on ten runs on two judges and one policy, and exposure predicts the first event, not the eventual winner.

candidates.why: An exact process oracle is a genuine enabling control and the padding-hack result is clean, but the fitted damage law does not travel to the independent reimplementation.
candidates.caveat: The headline damage law does not replicate — the branches rest on 6–7 cells from four verifiers.

candidates.why: Clean from-scratch paired design and a one-count take-off law, but the synthetic world is engineered so the RL problem is unusually clean.
candidates.caveat: The world is engineered so the RL problem is unusually clean — the step limit is chosen so the post-k-failure decision is the informative one.

candidates.why: Software fault injection into vLLM with a no-fault batch-composition null control separates harm from change, and shows all harm lands on ~11% fragile items (204/204 draws) while output-level detection is defeated.
candidates.caveat: Task spread is partly scoring-strictness, and all policy harm comes from 2 of 100 hand-written requests.

candidates.why: One-pass gradient sensitivity is a useful runtime win over exhaustive injection, but SimpleNet is indistinguishable from noise and validation is rank correlation only.
candidates.caveat: SimpleNet's global ρ = 0.12–0.20 is statistically indistinguishable from noise.

candidates.why: Permutation-invariance trick and BER-threshold curves are neat, but protection baselines are deliberate strawmen and each model sees exactly one GLUE task.
candidates.caveat: Baselines are only full Hamming-code and full TMR — nobody would protect an entire 1-bit weight array that way.

candidates.why: The 296/296 first-divergence margin result is a sharp mechanism finding, but it comes from one 0.6B model on one GPU/driver/PyTorch build.
candidates.caveat: The mechanism claim rests on a single GPU, single driver, single PyTorch/SDPA build.

candidates.why: 3,380 graded items, hashed preregistration, cluster bootstrap and a positive control: exact serving shortcuts flip 1.5–1.8% against a 1.72% reordering floor, while FP8 KV/weights double it — a noise-floor-anchored answer to 'does this shortcut matter'.
candidates.caveat: Statistical power constrains the headline: exactly three of seven features clear the floor, one by +0.05 pts.

candidates.why: Cross-vendor bitwise identity and elastic resizing are strong systems evidence, but the vendor-spanning test never exercises the split-reduction paths that are the actual contribution.
candidates.caveat: The cross-vendor test splits no reduction across GPUs, so it never exercises TP/DP/CP reduction paths.

candidates.why: 2,100 faulted runs over 8 tools and 9 fault types quantify fabrication (up to 38% under partial success), with payload-only sanitization and retry stratification inverting the naive story.
candidates.caveat: Fault type explains only ~6% of variance, and intention-to-treat pooling inflates the headline fabrication rates.

candidates.why: The 15-API silent-failure prevalence audit is valuable and the guard works, but the 74.0% → 1.7% headline is measured on the authors' own always-faulty mock servers.
candidates.caveat: Every fault repeats on every call on the authors' own servers with answers graded against their own oracle.

candidates.why: Receipt-proxying composition is well engineered, but live-trace accuracy is 76.67% with a 38.24% false-positive rate on only 60 traces.
candidates.caveat: Live MCP traces show 76.67% accuracy at a 38.24% false-positive rate on N=60.

candidates.why: Thorough (full 50k ImageNet, 46-arm screen, 328-point DP search) but single architecture/dataset with borrowed components and an internally inconsistent additivity claim; the area's slot goes to a pre-registered paired study.
candidates.caveat: The clipping and BN-recalibration gains are reported as individually equal yet jointly sub-additive, and the text is inconsistent about it.

candidates.why: Pre-registered paired design with blind human labels, three judges, equivalence margins and a format dose ladder shows 4-bit shifts refusal in opposite directions by model — the rare quantization study that can tell a null from an undetected effect.
candidates.caveat: The headline magnitude is not identified: the same contrast reads +6.2, +11.0 and +19.4 pp depending on judge.

candidates.why: The byte-identical unpruned control is the best part and cleanly attributes loops to pruning, but the method is incremental and its own ablation shows the gain is mostly wrong answers, not loops.
candidates.caveat: The headline method fails its own hypothesis — the 8-problem gain is mostly finished-wrong answers, not loops.

candidates.why: Stage-wise checkpoints plus layer stitching make a genuinely causal story about where readout breaks, but all three headline corpora are unreleasable and 'below chance' rests on graded log-odds under near-constant answers.
candidates.caveat: The central claim rests on corpora no reader can inspect, and in 23 of 36 conditions the model gave the same binary answer to >95% of texts.

candidates.why: 14 models, 227 human-validated minimal pairs, pre-registered equivalence bounds, random-head ablations and a 400-item external benchmark (37–39% of separation removed vs 1–3% for random) test moral-circuit specificity rather than assuming it.
candidates.caveat: The equivalence margin of 0.8–1.25 does the real work, and per-model intervals sit inside it in only 8/14 models.

candidates.why: Intervention discipline is good and the rule-failure/evidence-failure asymmetry is interesting, but the most quotable number rests on ~26 hallucination slots and controls are random directions only.
candidates.caveat: The headline hallucination number rests on roughly 26 slots, with no confidence intervals in Table 2.

candidates.why: A live production A/B (2,567 TPU repair windows, 225 H100) with per-family feature ablations and a longitudinal held-out set — rare deployment-scale evidence for a graph model replacing a hand-written rule engine.
candidates.caveat: The H100 A/B is under-powered (18.3% ± 7.6% on 225 windows), and symptom-only features match the full graph there, undercutting the transferable-prior claim.

candidates.why: SM-occupancy and host-CPU numbers are convincing, but the dramatic wins are against baselines the authors themselves call mismatched, and no BaM/CoPilotIO application comparison exists.
candidates.caveat: Application results compare only against bulk staging — no BaM or CoPilotIO column, which the authors call the principal remaining gap.

candidates.why: 30/30 wins over MegaMoE are real, but the margin is 1.05× on the flagship 2.4T configuration and the largest numbers come from the authors' own tuned re-implementations.
candidates.caveat: The 3.26×/3.62×/5.00× wins are against the authors' tuned re-implementations, with no upstream-code or second-implementation comparison.

candidates.why: A serious technical report with good serving ablations, but the capability comparison is unreliable — the best rows are exactly where the strongest competitors are dashes.
candidates.caveat: Missing-cell pattern in the coding table is not random, and the base-model table compares midtrained Beam against untrained baselines.

candidates.why: The full open release (checkpoints, data, synthesis pipelines) is a real contribution, but the flagship architecture ablation is a single confounded model pair and external baselines were re-run at unequal effort.
candidates.caveat: MoVA and softplus gating are introduced together in one model and compared against a different model, one run per arm.

candidates.why: A 'science-first' flagship with zero scientific benchmarks in its results table; the agentic wins are ≤1 task on 120-task subsets and harness-asymmetric.
candidates.caveat: Table 2 contains no scientific benchmark at all, and there is no ablation of the projector/GRPO interface.
